analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Alaska's two national forests as wilderness and bars logging and mining there.
analysis.headline: A bill to protect roughly 13 million acres of the Chugach and Tongass National Forests drew 124 cosponsors but was never granted a hearing or vote; it died quietly in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected vast parts of Alaska's Chugach and Tongass National Forests: about 6.9 million acres of new wilderness, another 5.8 million acres placed in a protective management category, plus restoration zones and dozens of wild and scenic rivers. Wilderness designation means no new roads, no clearcutting, and no mining or mineral leasing on those lands. The bill explicitly preserved hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and Alaska Native subsistence uses.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or values public lands: hunters, anglers, hikers, and campers who keep access under the bill's terms; Alaska residents who rely on subsistence hunting and fishing; and commercial and sport salmon fisheries whose streams would be shielded from clearcutting and road-building. Future generations keep the option of undeveloped forest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, subsistence users, and public-land visitors

how_it_helps.text: Designates about 3.66 million acres in the Chugach National Forest and about 3.23 million acres in the Tongass National Forest as wilderness, permanently off-limits to logging, road-building, and mining.
Places another 5.79 million acres of Tongass land in Land Use Designation II, a conservatively managed category, and directs that roaded portions within it be managed as restoration areas.

Declares Congress's intent to guarantee public use and enjoyment of these lands for hunting, fishing, hiking, and camping, and to preserve an opportunity for Alaskans to continue a subsistence way of life.
Adds dozens of river segments to the national wild and scenic rivers system and withdraws the lands along them from mining claims and mineral leasing, protecting salmon-producing watersheds.
Designates about 29,000 acres damaged by clearcutting and bad roads as restoration areas, requiring the Forest Service to close and rehabilitate roads and let the land recover.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the timber industry would lose access to old-growth stands in the Tongass, and mining and geothermal interests would lose the ability to stake claims and lease on the withdrawn lands. Some Southeast Alaska communities tied to logging and mining would face economic pressure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tongass timber operators and mining claimholders

drawbacks.text: Withdrawing roughly 13 million acres from logging and mining would reduce timber supply and mining opportunity, with real effects on jobs and revenue in some Southeast Alaska towns that depend on those industries.

Wilderness designation under the Wilderness Act bars roads, motorized vehicles, and mechanized equipment in designated areas, which some users see as locking them out of land they currently can reach.
Congressional designation of this much acreage in one bill leaves little flexibility for future managers to adjust to changed conditions, a common criticism of large wilderness bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are permanent and large, and the bill went out of its way to keep hunting, fishing, and subsistence access intact, so the public benefit is broad and durable. The costs fall on a narrow set of industries and on the communities around them, but those costs are real and concentrated in Southeast Alaska. A fairer process would have weighed both in committee and on the floor; that never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Resources Committee, passed along to its Forests and Forest Health subcommittee, and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing or vote, so it never reached the House floor and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Alaska Rainforest Conservation Act on February 27, 2003, with 123 original cosponsors.
It gathered 124 cosponsors in total — 120 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 3 Republicans.

The House referred it to the Committee on Resources on the day of introduction, and on March 10, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health; the subcommittee took no action.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber and mining interests that would have lost access to Tongass and Chugach lands, and the congressional leadership that preferred those lands stay open to logging and mining, were better off; the public kept no new protections and the lands remained available for development.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber and mining interests, and the committee leaders who stalled it

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized a large bipartisan-crossing cosponsor list at introduction.

for.name: 120 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad majority-party support in the House.

against.name: Richard Pombo
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: 3 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Only three House Republicans cosponsored, leaving the bill without the bipartisan weight that might have moved the majority-party committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 120 of the 124 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Independent and just 3 Republicans — and the Republican-run Resources Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Timber and logging companies (Tongass National Forest)
industries.note: The bill would end clearcutting on designated wilderness, restoration, and special management lands and close logging roads in restoration zones, cutting off access to old-growth timber that Southeast Alaska mills and operators depend on. Logging on public lands profits the industry at the cost of the forest the public owns.

Sections 603 and 705 withdraw wilderness, river corridors, and all designated areas from mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, ending any future claim-staking there. Public land is locked up for private mineral extraction under current rules.

industries.industry: Commercial and sport fishing, and Alaska recreation and tourism
industries.note: Protecting salmon-producing rivers and watersheds from clearcutting and roads supports fish runs, and designated wilderness keeps the landscape undeveloped for hunting, fishing, and visitors. The bill explicitly preserves those public uses.
